objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain why an instrument pilot notes every instrument and navigation equipment problem as it happens, describe the written records that must exist before the next IFR flight (squawks, deferrals, VOR checks, calibration and return-to-service entries), and teach a postflight routine that ends every lesson with a closed flight plan, clear write-ups and a learner-led debrief.
why: When shutting down the engine, the IFH asks the pilot to note any abnormal instrument indications [[23:133|IFH 5-38]], and a flight is not complete until the airplane is shut down and secured [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]. The owner must have discrepancies repaired between inspections [[60:520|14 CFR 91.405(a)]], and the next pilot in command decides whether the airplane is in condition for safe flight [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7(b)]]. Neither can act on a problem nobody wrote down, so your job is to make the write-up and the debrief as automatic as the before-takeoff checklist.

warmup: Think first: your instrument learner flew a good ILS today, but in the climb through the clouds the attitude indicator lagged in turns and the suction needle sat just below the green arc. After landing everything looks normal, and she wants to skip the write-up because "it works now." Tomorrow another pilot has the airplane booked for an IFR trip. What do you say to her, and what should be on paper before tomorrow's flight?

key_terms.def: A problem found with the airplane. After the flight, squawks and discrepancies should be noted and reported to maintenance [[24:349|AFH 17-15]].

The record provided for a pilot to enter a discrepancy; in the PHAK's MEL example the pilot makes the entry in the maintenance record or the discrepancy record [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]. Instructors should know the operator's procedure for reporting and correcting discrepancies and review the current discrepancy report [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

Under IFR in controlled airspace, the report to ATC of any in-flight malfunction of navigation, approach or communication equipment: aircraft identification, equipment affected, degree of impairment and assistance desired [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187]].

A user report of poor NAVAID or avionics performance, such as erratic course indications, flag alarms or a garbled identifier; GPS problems also go on the FAA GPS Anomaly Reporting Form after the flight [[33:87|AIM 1-1-13]] [[33:88|AIM 1-1-13]].

An approved list, with a letter of authorization, that allows takeoff with certain items inoperative; the aircraft records available to the pilot must include an entry describing them [[60:492|14 CFR 91.213(a)]].

Takeoff in a non-turbine airplane without an MEL with an item that is not VFR-day type-certification equipment and not required by the equipment list, KOEL, 91.205 or another Part 91 rule for that flight, or an AD; it is removed or deactivated and placarded, and a rated pilot or mechanic finds it is not a hazard [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]].

The marking placed near the switch, control or indicator of a deferred item [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]]. An inspector who finds items allowed inoperative placards them and adds them to the signed discrepancy list [[60:135|14 CFR 43.11(b)]].
After maintenance, no one may operate the airplane until a person authorized under 43.7 approves it for return to service and the 43.9 or 43.11 entry is made [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(a)]].

For IFR use of VOR, a check within the preceding 30 days: ±4° with a test signal or ground checkpoint, ±6° airborne, 4° between dual systems [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)]] [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(c)]], logged with date, place, bearing error and signature [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]].
A VOR test facility signal for checking a receiver on the ground: with the CDI centered, 0° FROM or 180° TO [[33:70|AIM 1-1-4]].

Test of the static system, altimeter and altitude reporting within the preceding 24 calendar months for IFR in controlled airspace, and again after the static system is opened and closed [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(a)]].
Learner self-assessment followed by the instructor's detailed assessment and a discussion that compares the two [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

chunks.title: What this Task asks, and why it ends every IFR lesson

body.p: **The Task.** The PTS asks you to describe two things: the **importance of noting instruments and navigation equipment for improper operation**, and the **reasons for making a written record of improper operation or failure and/or calibration of instruments prior to the next IFR flight** [[FAA-S-8081-9E:48|PTS X.A]]. Its FSTD appendix defines postflight procedures as closing flight plans, checking for discrepancies and malfunctions, and noting them on a log or maintenance form [[FAA-S-8081-9E:49|PTS Appendix 1]]. In its table for adding an instrument instructor rating, Area X is marked required in every column [[FAA-S-8081-9E:18|PTS Additional Rating Table]].

**Where the flight ends.** A flight is not complete until the engine is shut down and the airplane is secured [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]. At shutdown, note any abnormal instrument indications [[23:133|IFH 5-38]]. After the airplane is secured, do a complete post-flight inspection, and note any squawks or discrepancies and report them to maintenance [[24:349|AFH 17-15]].

**Why it belongs in every lesson.** The IFH's Instrument Training Lesson Guide lists "Postflight procedures" in almost every flight lesson, and says debriefing the student's performance is necessary to motivate further progress [[23:342|IFH B-1]] [[23:343|IFH B-2]]. Learners copy their instructor's habits, and safety practices mean little if the instructor does not demonstrate them consistently [[25:164|AIH 8-6]].

The Instrument lesson IR.VIII.A covers the pilot's side of this Task: the walkaround, servicing and the paperwork. The CFII lesson FII.III.C covers the check before flight and the go/no-go call for each item. This lesson joins the two: what the learner notices in flight, what must be written down before the next IFR flight, and how you teach it.

callout.text: Notice it, report it, write it, close it, debrief it.

check.q: Your learner asks why postflight procedures are on a CFII practical test at all. What do you say?
check.a: Because the next IFR flight depends on them. The PTS defines postflight procedures as closing flight plans, checking for discrepancies and malfunctions, and noting them on a log or maintenance form [[FAA-S-8081-9E:49|PTS Appendix 1]], and the owner must have discrepancies repaired between inspections [[60:520|14 CFR 91.405(a)]].

chunks.title: Noting improper operation: the flight instruments

body.p: **Importance of noting instruments for improper operation.** It is critical that all systems are found operational before departing into IFR conditions [[23:329|IFH 11-4]], and the pilot in command must discontinue the flight when unairworthy mechanical or electrical conditions occur [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7(b)]]. A pilot can only act on, and write up, what he or she noticed.

**Failures often start small.** Vacuum-driven attitude and heading indicators can fail progressively: as the gyros slow down they may wander [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]. When suction drops below the normal range, the gyros may become unstable and inaccurate [[1:218|PHAK 8-16]]. Many small airplanes have no vacuum failure warning, so the pilot should monitor the vacuum or pressure gauge [[23:332|IFH 11-7]] [[23:333|IFH 11-8]].

**How a failure shows.** A warning indicator, or a disagreement between the attitude indicator and the supporting performance instruments, usually identifies a failure [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]. Comparing the attitude indicator with the rate-of-turn indicator and VSI checks the static, suction and electrical systems against each other [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]. In Figure 11-8 the airplane is actually level at 2,000 feet; a pilot who misses the OFF flags may think it is turning left [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].

callout.text: Application: in a glass-panel airplane, have the learner name the standby instruments and the compass aloud in the cruise scan. The IFH says pilots drop them because the PFD is so reliable [[23:161|IFH 6-28]]. On a Cessna 172 the alternator light can hide behind open charts, so make sure it stays visible [[23:330|IFH 11-5]].

check.q: In cloud, your learner's attitude indicator shows a left bank, but the turn coordinator is level and the VSI reads zero. What do you teach?
check.a: Compare the attitude indicator with the turn indicator and VSI: the disagreement identifies the failure. Keep control on the working instruments, look for OFF flags, check the power source, and advise ATC [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]. Then note the time, conditions and suction reading for the write-up.

chunks.title: Noting improper operation: navigation and communication equipment

body.p: **Importance of noting navigation equipment for improper operation.** NAVAIDs are monitored by ground detectors, but interference, new obstructions or terrain changes near a NAVAID can degrade it without detection. Users are encouraged to report undesirable avionics performance [[33:87|AIM 1-1-13]]. What to watch for [[33:87|AIM 1-1-13]]:

bullets: Erratic course or bearing indications.
Intermittent or full flag alarm.
Garbled, missing or obviously improper coded identification.
Poor quality communications reception, or a hum or tone with frequency interference.
For GPS: navigation degradation or service loss indications.

body.p: **Rule out the airplane's own causes.** Some propeller rpm settings make the CDI fluctuate as much as ±6°, and a slight rpm change usually smooths it; pilots should check for this before reporting a VOR station or the aircraft equipment [[23:259|IFH 9-16]]. Never use a VOR reading taken while transmitting [[23:259|IFH 9-16]]. Some VORs show minor course roughness, and at a few stations, usually in mountainous terrain, the needle may briefly oscillate as if approaching the station [[23:259|IFH 9-16]].

**Faults that hide on the ground.** A receiver with a deteriorated gain control or modulation circuit can show acceptable accuracy close to a VOR or VOT and be out of tolerance farther away, where signals are weaker; periodic calibration is the best assurance [[33:71|AIM 1-1-4]]. Precipitation static builds with time in rain or snow until communication and navigation may become unusable [[23:328|IFH 11-3]]. So "it checked fine on the ground" does not prove the equipment works.

**Slaved compasses on the ramp.** Magnetic materials on or under taxiways and ramps can pull a slaved compass system off heading, and the error may not self-correct, so be alert for a misalignment and correct it before takeoff [[33:88|AIM 1-1-15]] [[33:89|AIM 1-1-15]]. Application: note where it happened, since a heading error after taxi may come from the ramp, not the airplane.

callout.text: Application: when the learner reports "the VOR was jumpy," ask four questions: which receiver, which station, what rpm, and did the other receiver agree? The answers decide whether you squawk the airplane, report the NAVAID, or both.

check.q: Your learner says the number 2 CDI swung about 5° each side all the way inbound and wants to squawk the radio. What do you check first?
check.a: Some propeller rpm settings cause CDI fluctuations up to ±6°, and a slight rpm change usually smooths it; the IFH asks pilots to check for this before reporting a VOR or the aircraft equipment [[23:259|IFH 9-16]]. Then compare with the other receiver on the same station.

chunks.title: Report it now: ATC and NAVAID reports

callout.text: The pilot in command of each aircraft operated in controlled airspace under IFR reports as soon as practical to ATC any malfunction of navigation, approach or communication equipment occurring in flight. The report includes (1) aircraft identification, (2) equipment affected, (3) the degree to which IFR capability in the ATC system is impaired, and (4) the nature and extent of assistance desired [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187]].

body.p: The AIM lists the same report, with the same four items, for any loss in controlled airspace of VOR, TACAN, ADF or low frequency receiver capability, GPS anomalies with an installed IFR GPS, complete or partial loss of ILS receiver capability, or impaired air/ground communications. Other equipment, such as weather radar, gets the same report if in the pilot's judgment it affects safety or IFR capability, and GPS reports include the location and altitude of the anomaly, and its duration if necessary [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3]]. For a vacuum or other instrument failure, the IFH says to advise ATC and, if necessary, declare an emergency [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].

Make the first report by radio to the controlling ATC facility or FSS, or by telephone to the nearest ATC facility for that airspace [[33:88|AIM 1-1-13]]. GPS problems should also be reported after the flight on the FAA GPS Anomaly Reporting Form [[33:88|AIM 1-1-13]]. Anomalies tied to a known GPS testing NOTAM are not reported in detail in flight unless they occur outside the NOTAMed area or have unexpected consequences [[33:88|AIM 1-1-13]].
**A useful anomaly report** contains [[33:87|AIM 1-1-13]] [[33:88|AIM 1-1-13]]:

bullets: Date and time, and the NAVAID ID (or GPS).
Where the aircraft was when the anomaly started and ended.
Heading, altitude and aircraft type and call sign.
The avionics in use, and the number of satellites tracked if applicable.
What happened and for how long, and its effect on the flight.
What the pilot did, what ATC provided, and the post flight pilot and maintenance actions taken.

body.p: **The radio call is not the write-up.** The ATC report helps this flight. The maintenance or discrepancy record is what reaches the owner and the next pilot [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

callout.text: Application: teach one short call that covers 91.187(b): "Center, Cessna 1230A, number one VOR has failed, able to continue IFR on GPS, no assistance needed." Then have the learner jot the time, position and altitude on the kneeboard for the write-up.

check.q: Under IFR in controlled airspace, in clear weather, your learner's ILS receiver fails. She says no report is needed because she can see the airport. What do you teach?
check.a: The rule covers any in-flight malfunction of navigation, approach or communication equipment under IFR in controlled airspace, whatever the weather: report it to ATC as soon as practical with identification, equipment, impairment and assistance wanted [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187]].

chunks.title: Why it must be written: who reads the record

body.p: **Reasons for making a written record of improper operation or failure.** First, the owner fixes what is written. The owner or operator is primarily responsible for keeping the airplane airworthy [[60:520|14 CFR 91.403(a)]] and must have discrepancies repaired between required inspections [[60:520|14 CFR 91.405(a)]]. The PHAK says the owner maintains airworthiness between inspections by having any defects corrected [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]].

**Second, the next pilot decides from it.** The pilot in command decides whether the airplane is in condition for safe flight [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7(b)]]. Logbooks are not normally kept in the airplane, so the pilot's procedure is to inspect the logbooks or a summary of the airworthy status before flight [[24:39|AFH 2-2]], and any discrepancies need to be addressed prior to flight [[24:41|AFH 2-4]].

**Third, the instructor reads it too.** Before scheduled flights, the instructor should determine the airplane's official airworthiness status, know the operator's procedure for reporting and correcting discrepancies, and review the current discrepancy report, ideally with the learner involved [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

check.q: A renter says squawks are the owner's problem, not his. How do you answer as his instructor?
check.a: The owner must have discrepancies repaired [[60:520|14 CFR 91.405(a)]] but cannot repair what was never reported. And the next pilot in command, maybe this renter, decides from the records whether the airplane is safe to fly [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7(b)]] [[24:39|AFH 2-2]].

chunks.title: The record decides the next IFR flight

body.p: Under 14 CFR, all instruments and installed equipment are required to be operative prior to each departure [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]]. With an inoperative item, the choice is to cancel, get maintenance, or defer it; deferrals are not used for in-flight discrepancies, which follow the AFM/POH [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]]. So the deferral decision is made on the ground, from what was written.

**With an MEL.** The airplane carries the approved MEL and letter of authorization, and the aircraft records available to the pilot must include an entry describing the inoperable items [[60:492|14 CFR 91.213(a)]]. In the PHAK example, the pilot makes an entry in the maintenance record or discrepancy record, and the item is then repaired or deferred under the MEL [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

**Without an MEL.** A non-turbine airplane may defer only an item that is not VFR-day type-certification equipment, not required by the equipment list or KOEL for the flight, not required by 91.205 or another Part 91 rule for that flight, and not required by an AD. It must be removed or deactivated and placarded, and a rated pilot or mechanic must find it is not a hazard [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]].

**What IFR adds.** For IFR, 91.205(d) requires the VFR-day items (and the VFR-night items at night), plus two-way radio and navigation equipment suitable for the route, a rate-of-turn indicator (unless a third attitude system is installed under 121.305(j)), a slip-skid indicator, a sensitive altimeter, a clock with seconds, an adequate generator or alternator, and attitude and heading indicators [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)]]. None of them can be deferred for an IFR flight [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iii)]]. FII.III.C has the item-by-item table.

**Then the owner's part.** Items allowed inoperative under 91.213(d)(2) are repaired, replaced, removed or inspected at the next required inspection [[60:521|14 CFR 91.405(c)]]. An inspector who finds the airplane unairworthy gives the owner a signed, dated list of discrepancies and placards the items allowed inoperative [[60:135|14 CFR 43.11(b)]]; the owner keeps that list until the defects are repaired and the airplane is approved for return to service [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(b)(3)]].

callout.text: An item that cannot be deferred and cannot be repaired on the field may be flown to a repair shop only under a special flight permit [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(e)]] [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

check.q: After a training flight your learner squawks a heading indicator whose failure flag will not clear. The next renter wants to placard it and fly IFR tomorrow. What do you say?
check.a: A gyroscopic direction indicator is required for IFR [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(9)]], and an item 91.205 requires for that flight cannot be deferred under 91.213(d) [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iii)]]. It needs repair and a return-to-service entry before IFR [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(a)]].

chunks.title: Calibration records: VOR, altimeter, transponder and compass

body.p: **Reasons for a written record of calibration.** Some records prove an instrument is accurate, not just working, and the next pilot can only check them on paper. The pilot's airworthiness check includes the 30-day VOR check and the 24-month transponder, static system and encoder tests [[24:40|AFH 2-3]], and the IFH has the pilot confirm the altimeter and static tests in the aircraft records [[23:131|IFH 5-36]].

body.p: **The habit, from the IFH sample flight.** A quick check of the logbooks shows the altimeter, static and transponder tests within 24 calendar months, and a log on the clipboard shows the VOR checked within the preceding 30 days [[23:321|IFH 10-30]] [[23:322|IFH 10-31]]. With an error over ±4° on a ground check or ±6° airborne, IFR flight must not be attempted until the source is corrected, and no correction other than the manufacturer's correction card may be applied [[33:71|AIM 1-1-4]]. Yearly receiver calibration by an authorized repair facility is recommended [[33:71|AIM 1-1-4]].

callout.text: Application: on days you pass a VOT or checkpoint, make the VOR check part of the postflight flow and have the learner write the entry while you watch. A check that is done but not logged does not meet 91.171(d) [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]].

check.q: Your learner checks the VOR at a VOT: CDI centered with the OBS at 357° and a FROM flag. What goes in the log?
check.a: A perfect VOT check reads 0° FROM [[33:70|AIM 1-1-4]], so the bearing error is 3°, within ±4° [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(1)]]. She enters the date, place and bearing error and signs the aircraft log or other record [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]].

chunks.title: After the fix: what must exist before the next IFR flight

body.p: A squawk starts a loop that closes only with an entry. No one may operate an airplane after maintenance until a person authorized under 43.7 approves it for return to service and the 43.9 or 43.11 entry is made [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(a)]]. The owner must make sure maintenance personnel make those entries [[60:521|14 CFR 91.405(b)]].

Some work needs more. If maintenance may have appreciably changed the flight characteristics or substantially affected operation in flight, no passengers may be carried until a pilot with at least a private certificate flies an operational check and logs it in the aircraft records [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(b)]], unless ground tests or inspection show conclusively that it was not affected [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(c)]].

For IFR, watch for two follow-on tests. A static system that was opened and closed must be tested again before IFR in controlled airspace, except for use of the drains and alternate static valve [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(a)(2)]]. Transponder work that could introduce a data correspondence error needs the integrated system tested [[60:525|14 CFR 91.413(b)]].
What the learner checks in the records before the next IFR flight:

bullets: Each open squawk has a matching return-to-service entry [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(a)]].
Any deferred item is placarded, and its removal or any deactivation that involved maintenance is recorded [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(3)]].
The VOR check is within 30 days and logged [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]].
The altimeter, static, encoder and transponder tests are within 24 calendar months [[24:40|AFH 2-3]].

callout.text: Preventive maintenance is limited to the items in Part 43 appendix A(c) [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]. Application: send instrument and avionics problems to maintenance; the pilot's job is a clear write-up.

check.q: A mechanic replaced a leaking static line yesterday and signed the airplane off. Your learner plans an IFR flight in controlled airspace. What else do you look for?
check.a: A static system test and inspection after the system was opened and closed [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(a)(2)]], besides the return-to-service entry [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(a)]].

body.p: The PTS lists closing flight plans first among postflight procedures [[FAA-S-8081-9E:49|PTS Appendix 1]]. When a flight plan has been activated, the pilot in command must notify an FSS or ATC facility on canceling or completing the flight under it [[60:470|14 CFR 91.169(d)]] [[60:464|14 CFR 91.153(b)]].

body.p: Why it matters: an open IFR plan holds airspace other IFR traffic could use [[23:294|IFH 10-3]] [[33:340|AIM 5-1-15]], and an open VFR plan sends searchers after a pilot who is safe on the ground; close it immediately after arrival [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]].

callout.text: Application: practice approaches at a nontowered field make a good teaching point. Before the last approach, ask the learner how she will cancel if her radio cannot reach ATC on the ground, and have her say the call.

check.q: Your learner lands at a towered airport on an IFR flight plan and asks how to close it. What do you say?
check.a: With an operating control tower, the IFR flight plan is closed automatically on landing [[33:340|AIM 5-1-15]] [[23:294|IFH 10-3]]. VFR plans are different: the pilot closes those, because towers do not [[33:339|AIM 5-1-14]].

body.p: **Start on lesson one.** Correct habit patterns from the beginning are essential [[25:91|AIH 3-40]]. Primacy is a fundamental principle of learning, so the instructor insists on correct procedures from the outset; it is much easier to build good habits than to correct faulty ones later [[25:91|AIH 3-40]]. The IFH lesson guide puts postflight procedures into almost every flight lesson [[23:342|IFH B-1]] [[23:344|IFH B-3]].

**Model it.** Learners see the instructor as a role model whose habits they imitate, consciously or not [[25:164|AIH 8-6]]. If you walk away from the airplane without writing up the flickering flag, the learner will too.
Application: one postflight flow, in this order:

bullets: 1. At shutdown, note any abnormal instrument indications [[23:133|IFH 5-38]].
2. Post-flight inspection, servicing and securing [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].
3. Close or confirm the flight plan [[33:340|AIM 5-1-15]].
4. Write the squawks and log any VOR check [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]] [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]].
5. Debrief: learner self-assessment first, then your assessment and a comparison [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

body.p: **Debrief with the four Rs.** Replay: the learner tells the flight back while you listen for parts that do not seem accurate. Reconstruct: what the learner would, could or should have done differently. Reflect: what was learned, what was easiest and hardest, what was uncomfortable. Redirect: relate today's lesson to other experiences and future sessions [[25:136|AIH 6-5]]. Write your critique as notes, so you cover every area you noticed [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

Self-assessment builds the habit of healthy reflection and self-assessment that is critical to being a safe pilot [[25:138|AIH 6-7]]. Risk management belongs in all preflight and postflight briefings, and learners should be encouraged to lead those discussions as their experience grows [[25:186|AIH 10-2]]. As the learner gains knowledge, he or she should lead the postflight review while you guide it with targeted questions [[25:119|AIH 5-16]].

callout.text: Application: add one fixed question to every instrument debrief: "Did any instrument or radio do anything odd today, and is it written down?" Over time the learner asks it before you do.

check.q: Ten lessons in, your learner still waits for you to start the squawk sheet. How do you move the habit to her?
check.a: Have her lead the postflight review while you guide with targeted questions [[25:119|AIH 5-16]], start each debrief with her self-assessment [[25:182|AIH 9-12]], and keep modeling the write-up yourself, since learners imitate the instructor's habits [[25:164|AIH 8-6]].

chunks.title: Writing a useful squawk, and common learner errors

body.p: **What a squawk needs.** No source here gives a squawk sheet format, but the AIM's anomaly report shows what a useful report contains: when, where it started and ended, heading and altitude, the equipment in use, what happened and for how long, the effect, and what was done [[33:87|AIM 1-1-13]] [[33:88|AIM 1-1-13]]. Teach the learner to describe symptoms and conditions, not to diagnose.

head: Weak squawk
Application: a better one
rows: "AI bad."
"Attitude indicator showed about 10° left bank with turn coordinator level, 20 minutes into IMC at 6,000 ft. Suction just below the green arc. Normal on the ground after landing."
"VOR 2 jumpy."
"NAV 2 CDI swung about 5° each side on the ABC 090 radial inbound, 4,000 ft, at 2,400 and 2,200 rpm. NAV 1 steady on the same radial."
"Radio weak."
"COM 2 transmissions unreadable to approach and tower; COM 1 normal. Receive normal on both."

body.p: **Common learner errors.**

bullets: "It works now." The AIH warns of a natural tendency to explain away errors as one-time events [[25:86|AIH 3-35]]. Learners do the same with an instrument that misbehaved once and then recovered.
Telling ATC but writing nothing. The 91.187 report serves this flight [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187]]; the discrepancy record reaches the owner and the next pilot [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].
Hurrying the postflight. Under pressure a pilot may do a cursory inspection to save time, only to have a problem show up later [[25:85|AIH 3-34]].
Calling a placard a deferral without checking type certification, the equipment list, KOEL, 91.205 and ADs, and without the hazard determination [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]].
Fixing it themselves. Preventive maintenance is limited to the Part 43 appendix A(c) items, and a pilot who does it must make a maintenance record entry [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].
Doing the VOR check but not logging date, place, bearing error and signature [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]].

callout.text: Application: grade the squawk like any other task. Ask, "Could a mechanic reproduce this from what you wrote?" If not, the learner rewrites it before leaving.

check.q: Your learner writes "GPS weird" on the squawk sheet after the GPS showed an integrity alert for ten minutes near a military area. What do you have her add?
check.a: When and where it started and ended, altitude and heading, the unit in use, what it showed and for how long, the effect and what she did [[33:87|AIM 1-1-13]] [[33:88|AIM 1-1-13]]. GPS problems should also be reported after the flight on the FAA GPS Anomaly Reporting Form [[33:88|AIM 1-1-13]].

chunks.title: Risk: the inoperative item and the next IFR flight

body.p: Inoperative equipment triggers an "A" hazard, so consider its effect in relation to the expected flight conditions [[30:25|RMH 3-7]]. Redundancy matters more in IMC: one radio is not a major concern on a day VFR flight but could be an "A" hazard in IMC, and instrument failure is a concern in IMC or at night [[30:24|RMH 3-6]].

Deferral is not to be taken lightly; consider the effect of an inoperative item on the operation, particularly if other items are also inoperative [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]. If you find a discrepancy and hear yourself say it is "probably" okay to fly, revisit the consequences [[1:56|PHAK 2-17]].

A postflight inspection can find aircraft hazards before the next person flies [[30:22|RMH 3-4]], and addressing discrepancies and proper maintenance increase reliability and reduce risk [[30:39|RMH 5-1]]. Once the airplane is secured, a good post-flight analysis reviews the flight objectively, so mistakes and judgment errors are recognized and learned from before the next flight [[1:57|PHAK 2-18]].

callout.text: Legal is not the same as safe. An autopilot is not on the 91.205 list [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)]], but flying IMC without one raises workload and can be an "A" hazard [[30:24|RMH 3-6]].

Application: the PTS verb is "describing," so expect oral questions in a scenario: "You landed and the number 2 nav was flagging. What do you do now, and can your student fly IFR tomorrow?" Answer in the order of this lesson: report, write, defer or fix, records, debrief.

check.q: The landing light failed on today's flight, and it is not required for your learner's Part 91 night IFR trip tomorrow. What do you teach?
check.a: Legal is only the first question. Inoperative equipment is still an "A" hazard; the RMH uses this exact example, and the pilot weighs its effect against the expected conditions [[30:25|RMH 3-7]].

scenario.title: A vacuum pump on its way out
scenario.setup: You are a CFII. Your instrument learner flies a club airplane with a six-pack panel, one vacuum pump, two nav/coms and an IFR GPS. Today's plan: an IFR flight plan to a nontowered airport 40 miles away in a 1,200-foot overcast, a full stop there, then VFR home under the clouds. Climbing through the overcast, the suction needle sits just below the green arc and the attitude indicator lags in turns. On the VOR approach the number 2 CDI wanders a few degrees each side. After landing everything looks normal. Another club member has the airplane booked tomorrow for an IFR trip.

questions.q: In the clouds, what should your learner be doing about the suction reading and the lagging attitude indicator?
questions.a: Watch the suction gauge, since many small airplanes have no vacuum warning [[23:332|IFH 11-7]] [[23:333|IFH 11-8]], and expect the gyros to become unstable and inaccurate with low suction [[1:218|PHAK 8-16]]. Cross-check the attitude indicator against the turn indicator and VSI, and if it fails, advise ATC [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]. Note the time and readings for the write-up.

questions.q: The number 2 CDI wanders on the approach. What do you teach before anyone calls it a failure?
questions.a: Try a slight rpm change, since some rpm settings cause fluctuations up to ±6° [[23:259|IFH 9-16]], and compare with number 1 on the same station. If the receiver really has malfunctioned under IFR in controlled airspace, report it to ATC with the four items [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187]]. If it looks like the station, a NAVAID report helps [[33:87|AIM 1-1-13]].

questions.q: On the ground at the nontowered airport, your radio cannot reach ATC and there is no FSS on the field. How should the IFR flight plan have been closed?
questions.a: The pilot must cancel at a nontowered field. With no FSS or direct contact on the ground, the AIM says to cancel while still airborne and in radio contact, weather permitting [[33:340|AIM 5-1-15]], and only if the rest of the flight can be VFR [[23:294|IFH 10-3]]. If it is still open, cancel by telephone now [[23:294|IFH 10-3]].

questions.q: Back home the attitude indicator looks fine. What goes on the squawk sheet, and why can it not wait?
questions.a: Both items, with conditions, times, altitude, readings and what was done [[33:87|AIM 1-1-13]] [[33:88|AIM 1-1-13]], in the discrepancy record [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]. The owner must have discrepancies repaired [[60:520|14 CFR 91.405(a)]], and tomorrow's pilot in command decides airworthiness from the record [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7(b)]]. The attitude indicator is required for IFR [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(8)]].

questions.q: Tomorrow's pilot calls: maintenance replaced the vacuum pump this morning. What should he see in the records before he files IFR?
questions.a: The approval for return to service and the 43.9 entry [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(a)]]. If he will use VOR under IFR, a VOR check within the preceding 30 days, logged with date, place, bearing error and signature [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(a)]] [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]], plus the 24-month altimeter, static and transponder tests [[24:40|AFH 2-3]]. He should also see what was done about the number 2 nav write-up: repaired with a return-to-service entry, or properly deferred if nothing requires it [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]].

questions.q: How do you run today's debrief?
questions.a: Learner self-assessment first, with replay, reconstruct, reflect and redirect [[25:136|AIH 6-5]], then compare it with your written notes [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Include the risk discussion [[25:186|AIH 10-2]], and as she gains knowledge let her lead the review [[25:119|AIH 5-16]].

skills.do: Explain aloud, as you would to a learner in the airplane, how you notice improper operation of the flight instruments and navigation equipment in flight: what to cross-check, how to tell an airplane fault from a station fault, and what to report to ATC.
skills.practice: Fly or simulate a short IFR trip with another applicant as your learner. At each odd indication, talk through the IFH comparison of attitude indicator, turn indicator and VSI [[23:332|IFH 11-7]], the rpm check for a wandering CDI [[23:259|IFH 9-16]], and a 91.187 report with its four items [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187(b)]].

skills.do: Run a postflight debrief out loud: close the flight plan, write a squawk a mechanic could act on, log a VOR check, and explain why each record must exist before the next IFR flight.
skills.practice: With a partner, take three sample discrepancies, write each as a squawk, decide whether the airplane can go IFR under 91.205(d) and 91.213(d) [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)]] [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]], and finish with a four-R debrief [[25:136|AIH 6-5]].

quiz.q: Your learner sees the suction needle just below the green arc in cruise, but the gyros look normal. What does the PHAK say?
options: Low suction matters only during the engine run-up
The gyros may become unstable and inaccurate
Low suction affects only the electric turn coordinator
Ignore it as long as the two gyros agree with each other
quiz.why: When vacuum pressure drops below the normal range, the gyroscopic instruments may become unstable and inaccurate [[1:218|PHAK 8-16]], and many small airplanes have no vacuum warning, so the gauge is the warning [[23:333|IFH 11-8]]. In some airplanes the turn coordinator runs on electric power, so low suction does not affect it [[1:218|PHAK 8-16]].

quiz.q: In IMC your learner's attitude indicator shows a left bank, but the turn coordinator is level and the VSI reads zero. What does the IFH teach to find the failure?
options: Compare the attitude indicator with the turn indicator and VSI
Trust the attitude indicator, the only direct attitude reference
Tap the panel and wait for the gyro to erect itself again
Select alternate static and see which instruments change
quiz.why: A disagreement between the attitude indicator and the supporting instruments usually identifies the failure; comparing it with the rate-of-turn indicator and VSI checks the suction, static and electrical systems against each other [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]. Alternate static fixes a static blockage, not a gyro failure [[23:333|IFH 11-8]].

quiz.q: Inbound on a VOR radial, your learner's CDI swings about 5° each side. Before she reports the VOR or the receiver, what does the IFH say to check?
options: Whether the OBS is set to the reciprocal
Whether a VOT can be received in flight
Whether a small rpm change smooths it
Whether the transponder is interfering with it
quiz.why: Some propeller rpm settings make the CDI fluctuate as much as ±6°, and a slight rpm change usually smooths it; pilots should check for this before reporting a VOR or the aircraft equipment [[23:259|IFH 9-16]]. Airborne VOT use is limited to areas authorized in the Chart Supplement [[33:70|AIM 1-1-4]].

quiz.q: Under IFR in controlled airspace but in clear weather, your learner's ILS receiver fails. What does 14 CFR 91.187 require?
options: No report, since she can see the airport
A report to ATC as soon as practical
A written report to the FSDO afterward
A report only if she declares an emergency
quiz.why: The pilot in command of an aircraft under IFR in controlled airspace reports any in-flight malfunction of navigation, approach or communication equipment to ATC as soon as practical [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187(a)]]. The rule says nothing about the weather, so seeing the airport does not remove the duty.

quiz.q: Your learner calls: "Center, Cessna 1230A, number one VOR has failed." Under 91.187, what did she leave out?
options: Her position, altitude and the time it failed
The VOR frequency and the last radial tracked
Her fuel remaining and persons on board
How IFR is impaired and the help she wants
quiz.why: A 91.187 report includes aircraft identification, the equipment affected, the degree to which IFR capability is impaired, and the nature and extent of assistance desired [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187(b)]]. Position and time are good notes for the write-up, but they are not among the four required items.

quiz.q: Your learner asks why pilots should report a NAVAID that acts up, since the FAA monitors NAVAIDs. What does the AIM say?
options: Ground monitors can miss interference, new obstructions or terrain changes
Monitors work only during the hours the local FSS is open
Pilot reports replace the FAA's flight inspection program
Monitors check only the identifier, not the course signal
quiz.why: NAVAIDs are monitored by electronic detectors, but interference, new obstructions or terrain changes near the NAVAID can exist without detection by the ground monitors, so users are encouraged to report undesirable performance [[33:87|AIM 1-1-13]].

quiz.q: A renter says squawks are the owner's problem. Which rule makes the owner's job depend on what pilots write up?
options: 91.409(a): an annual inspection within the preceding 12 calendar months
91.411(a): a static system test every 24 calendar months
91.405(a): have discrepancies repaired between inspections
91.171(a): a VOR check within the preceding 30 days
quiz.why: The owner or operator must, between required inspections, have discrepancies repaired [[60:520|14 CFR 91.405(a)]], and cannot repair what nobody reported. The inspection and test rules run on the calendar, not on pilot reports [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(a)]] [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(a)]].

quiz.q: Your club's airplane has an approved MEL and letter of authorization. The number 2 nav radio fails and is deferred under the MEL. What must the records available to the pilot include?
options: A special flight permit for each flight
An FAA Form 337 for the deferral
Nothing more, since the MEL covers it
An entry describing the inoperable item
quiz.why: With an MEL, the aircraft records available to the pilot must include an entry describing the inoperable instruments and equipment [[60:492|14 CFR 91.213(a)(4)]]. A special flight permit is for items that cannot be deferred [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(e)]].

quiz.q: At the VOT your learner centers the CDI with the OBS at 177° and a TO flag. What does she log?
options: Nothing: a TO check must read exactly 180°
Date, place, 3° bearing error, her signature
Only her initials; a VOT needs no error figure
Nothing: only a repair station logs a VOT check
quiz.why: A perfect VOT check reads 180° TO [[33:70|AIM 1-1-4]], so 177° is a 3° error, within ±4° [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(1)]]. The person making the check enters the date, place and bearing error and signs the record [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]]; a repair station adds its own entry only when its radiated test signal is used.

quiz.q: A mechanic replaced a cracked static line and signed the airplane off. Before IFR in controlled airspace, what else must be done?
options: A static system test
Nothing, since the 24-month test is current
A pilot check that the altimeter reads field elevation
A new VOR check, since the panel was disturbed
quiz.why: After any opening and closing of the static system, other than the drains and alternate static valve, the system must be tested and inspected before IFR in controlled airspace [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(a)(2)]]. A current 24-month test does not cover the new work.

quiz.q: Your learner lands at a towered airport on an IFR flight plan. How is the flight plan closed?
options: She calls FSS within 30 minutes of landing
Ground control closes it when she asks for taxi
It closes automatically when she has landed
She must cancel on the tower frequency before landing
quiz.why: On an IFR flight plan to an airport with a functioning control tower, the flight plan is closed automatically upon landing [[33:340|AIM 5-1-15]] [[23:294|IFH 10-3]]. The 30-minute rule belongs to VFR flight plans [[33:339|AIM 5-1-14]].

quiz.q: Your instrument learner is well into the course. How does the AIH suggest the postflight review should change?
options: Shorten it to a grade sheet signed in the office
Stop debriefing once she flies to the standards
Have her write a summary that you read later
She leads it; you guide with targeted questions
quiz.why: As the learner grows in flight knowledge, he or she should be able to lead the postflight review while the instructor guides the discussion with targeted questions [[25:119|AIH 5-16]]. The instructor still compares assessments in a discussion, not on paper alone [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner says the VOR passed at the VOT, so the receiver can't be why the needle wandered 60 miles out. What does the AIM say?
options: A worn receiver can pass close in and fail farther out
A VOT pass proves accuracy at all ranges for 30 days
Errors far from a station come only from the station
Receivers drift only after an airborne check has failed
final_quiz.why: If a receiver's gain control or modulation circuit deteriorates, it can show acceptable accuracy close to the VOR or VOT and out-of-tolerance readings farther away, where signals are weaker; periodic calibration is the best assurance [[33:71|AIM 1-1-4]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner lands on an IFR flight plan at a nontowered field with no FSS and no radio contact with ATC on the ground. What should she have done?
options: Left it open, since an IFR plan closes itself 30 minutes after ETA
Canceled airborne in VFR while still in radio contact
Set 7600 on the ground to show ATC she landed
Asked the next airport's tower to close it later
final_quiz.why: At an airport without a functioning tower the pilot must cancel; with no FSS or radio contact on the ground, cancel while still airborne and able to talk to ATC, weather permitting [[33:340|AIM 5-1-15]], and be certain the rest of the flight can be VFR [[23:294|IFH 10-3]]. IFR plans to nontowered fields do not close themselves.

final_quiz.q: Your learner lands at a towered airport on a VFR flight plan. Who closes it?
options: The tower, automatically, on landing
Ground control, when she calls for taxi
She does, with FSS or by an ATC relay
No one; VFR plans lapse at the ETA
final_quiz.why: The pilot is responsible for closing a VFR or DVFR flight plan with FSS, or by asking an ATC facility to relay; towers do not close them automatically, and search and rescue starts if it is not closed within 1/2 hour after ETA [[33:339|AIM 5-1-14]]. Only IFR plans close automatically at a towered airport [[33:340|AIM 5-1-15]].

final_quiz.q: No MEL. After the flight your learner finds the clock's second hand has stopped. Can the next pilot placard it and fly IFR?
options: Yes, once a rated pilot finds it is not a hazard
Yes, if the KOEL does not list a clock at all
Yes, once the failure is in the discrepancy record
No: 91.205(d) requires it; it cannot be deferred
final_quiz.why: IFR requires a clock showing hours, minutes and seconds [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(6)]], and an item required by 91.205 for that kind of flight cannot be deferred under 91.213(d), no matter what the KOEL or a hazard determination says [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iii)]].

final_quiz.q: No MEL. Which inoperative item could be deferred under 91.213(d) for an IFR flight, if type certification, the equipment list, KOEL and ADs allow?
options: The autopilot
The attitude indicator
The slip-skid indicator
The alternator
final_quiz.why: The attitude indicator, slip-skid indicator and an adequate generator or alternator are all on the 91.205(d) list for IFR; an autopilot is not [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)]]. Items 91.205 requires cannot be deferred [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iii)]]. Flying IMC without the autopilot is still an extra workload to weigh [[30:24|RMH 3-6]].

final_quiz.q: At the annual, the inspector finds the RMI inoperative but allowed under 91.213(d)(2). What must the owner end up with?
options: A special flight permit for each flight until it is fixed
A signed, dated discrepancy list; RMI placarded
A new supplemental type certificate
Nothing in writing until the next annual
final_quiz.why: The inspector gives the owner a signed, dated list of discrepancies and placards each item allowed inoperative under 91.213(d)(2) [[60:135|14 CFR 43.11(b)]]. The owner keeps that list until the defects are repaired [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(b)(3)]] and has the item fixed or inspected at the next required inspection [[60:521|14 CFR 91.405(c)]].

final_quiz.q: The departure airport has no VOT or ground checkpoint. Over the airborne checkpoint, published as the 160° radial, the receiver shows 165°. What does your learner do?
options: Fail it, since anything over 4° fails
Apply a 5° correction on every radial
Pass it within ±6°, then log the check
Skip the log; airborne checks aren't logged
final_quiz.why: An airborne checkpoint is used when no test signal or ground checkpoint is available, and its limit is ±6° [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(3)]], so 5° passes, and every check is logged with date, place, bearing error and signature [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]]. The ±4° limit is for ground checks, and no correction other than the manufacturer's card may be applied [[33:71|AIM 1-1-4]].

final_quiz.q: On the ramp your learner's altimeter reads 95 feet above field elevation; in the run-up area it still reads 90 feet high. What does the IFH say?
options: Reset the needles to field elevation and go
Accept it, since only ramp height is off
Only errors of 100 feet or more matter
Refer it to a repair station
final_quiz.why: If the altimeter is not within 75 feet of field elevation, its accuracy is questionable and it should be referred to a repair station; the recheck in the run-up area rules out a ramp that differs from field elevation [[23:132|IFH 5-37]] [[23:100|IFH 5-5]].

final_quiz.q: COM 2 was unreadable to approach, but COM 1 worked fine. Your learner wants to skip the write-up. What is the best reason not to?
options: The next pilot may plan IMC on one radio without knowing
COM radios must be tested every 24 calendar months
ATC requires a written follow-up within 24 hours
The tower will not close her flight plan without it
final_quiz.why: In IMC, having one radio could be an "A" hazard [[30:24|RMH 3-6]], and the next pilot in command decides airworthiness from the records [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7(b)]] [[24:39|AFH 2-2]]. The 24-month test rule is for transponders, not com radios [[60:525|14 CFR 91.413(a)]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner says the attitude indicator "only acted up once" and works now, so there is nothing to write up. Which AIH idea do you point to?
options: Primacy: what is learned first is learned best
Explaining errors away as just one-time events
Positive transfer from the full-panel lessons
The speed-accuracy tradeoff under time pressure
final_quiz.why: The AIH warns of a natural tendency to "explain away" errors, dismissing them as one-time events that will likely never happen again [[25:86|AIH 3-35]]. The same pull hides an intermittent instrument. Primacy is about building correct habits from the start [[25:91|AIH 3-40]], which is why you insist on the write-up.

final_quiz.q: In the four-R debrief, which step asks what the learner would, could or should have done differently?
options: Replay
Reflect
Reconstruct
Redirect
final_quiz.why: Reconstruct identifies the key things the learner would have, could have or should have done differently. Replay retells the flight, Reflect finds meaning, and Redirect links the lesson to future sessions [[25:136|AIH 6-5]].

final_quiz.q: Why does the AIH have the learner self-assess before you give your assessment?
options: It saves time, since you then need no notes
It lets the learner set the lesson grade
It replaces the written postflight critique
It builds the habit of healthy reflection
final_quiz.why: Involving the learner in assessment establishes the habit of healthy reflection and self-assessment that is critical to being a safe pilot [[25:138|AIH 6-7]]. The instructor still keeps written notes and compares the two assessments [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

final_quiz.q: A mechanic installed a new attitude indicator but has not made the logbook entry yet. Your learner wants to go IFR now. What do you say?
options: Not until it is approved and the entry is made
Fine, if the new gyro erects on the run-up
Fine, if the mechanic says the work is done
Fine, as long as she carries no passengers
final_quiz.why: No one may operate an airplane after maintenance until it is approved for return to service and the 43.9 or 43.11 entry is made [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(a)]]. The no-passengers rule is a separate test-flight rule for work that may change flight characteristics [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(b)]].

final_quiz.q: After a flight with a flickering nav flag, your learner asks why the debrief covers "what if it had failed in cloud." What does the AIH say?
options: Risk talk belongs only in the preflight briefing
Risk management belongs in all postflight briefs too
The FRAT covers risk, so the debrief need not
Risk is reviewed only at stage checks
final_quiz.why: Risk management activity and discussion should be included in all preflight and postflight briefings, and learners should be encouraged to lead them as experience grows [[25:186|AIH 10-2]].

final_quiz.q: The landing light is inoperative, and it is not required for your learner's Part 91 night flight. What does the RMH say?
options: It is legal, so it is not a hazard at all
It must be repaired before any night flight
It is still an "A" hazard to weigh
It matters only on a VFR flight at night
final_quiz.why: Inoperative equipment triggers an "A" hazard; an inoperative landing light may make night operation more hazardous even though it is not required for Part 91 flights not for hire, so weigh it against the expected conditions [[30:25|RMH 3-7]].

takeaways: Note it when it happens: time, place, altitude, readings and what you did.
Find a failure by comparison: attitude indicator against turn indicator and VSI; watch the suction and the ammeter.
Before blaming a VOR, change rpm and compare receivers; a VOT pass does not prove accuracy far from the station.
Under IFR in controlled airspace, report nav, approach or comm malfunctions to ATC: ID, equipment, impairment, help wanted.
Write it down: the owner fixes what is written and the next pilot decides from it. Nothing on the 91.205(d) list can be deferred for IFR.
Log the VOR check (date, place, error, signature); check the 24-month tests and the return-to-service entries.
Close the flight plan: automatic under IFR at a towered field; the pilot's job at a nontowered field and for every VFR plan.
End every lesson the same way: learner self-assessment with the four Rs, then your notes and a comparison.
cfi_notes: The PTS lists the Instrument ACS and the AFM as references, and its FSTD appendix defines postflight procedures as closing flight plans, checking for discrepancies and malfunctions, and noting them on a log or maintenance form [[FAA-S-8081-9E:48|PTS X.A]] [[FAA-S-8081-9E:49|PTS Appendix 1]]. The objective verb is "describing," so expect oral, scenario questions; the table for adding an instrument instructor rating marks Area X as required in every column [[FAA-S-8081-9E:18|PTS Additional Rating Table]].

IFH 9-16 says the VOR check needs "an appropriate endorsement" within 30 days and sends pilots to the A/FD [[23:259|IFH 9-16]]. The rule requires a log entry with date, place, bearing error and signature [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]], and the AIM now names the Chart Supplement [[33:71|AIM 1-1-4]]. Teach the rule's wording.

Who swings the compass: IFH 5-12 and 5-13 say "a pilot or AMT" swings it and adjusts the compensating magnets [[23:107|IFH 5-12]] [[23:108|IFH 5-13]], while PHAK 8-25 says only AMTs can adjust the compass or complete the correction card, and the pilot may taxi the airplane onto the compass rose headings [[1:227|PHAK 8-25]]. Teach the PHAK, as FII.III.C does: the pilot writes it up and maintenance fixes it.

Deactivation: PHAK 9-10 says it may be as simple as the pilot positioning a circuit breaker to OFF, while complex deactivation needs a certificated, appropriately rated maintenance person, and removal always involves maintenance [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]] [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]; the rule says deactivation that involves maintenance must be done and recorded under Part 43 [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(3)(ii)]]. Neither says exactly where that line falls. AC 91-67A, which the Instrument lesson IR.VIII.A uses, is not a build source here; agree the school's procedure with its maintenance shop.

91.187 covers navigation, approach and communication equipment only [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187(a)]]. For a vacuum or other instrument failure, the IFH says to advise ATC and declare an emergency if necessary [[23:332|IFH 11-7]], and the AIM asks for a report on any other equipment that affects safety or IFR capability [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3]].

The AFH's clearest squawk sentence sits in its light-sport chapter: note squawks and discrepancies, report them to maintenance, and insist on a debriefing with critique and planning for the next lesson [[24:349|AFH 17-15]]. It fits an IFR trainer just as well.

Application: practice this Task joined to an emergency Task, such as a partial-panel approach in Area IX: report the failure, write it up, decide on the next IFR flight and debrief the "student," all aloud. An examiner can test the whole chain in one scenario.

Records of the 24-month tests: 91.417(a) leaves work done under 91.411 and 91.413 out of the maintenance records the owner must keep [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(a)]], yet the IFH and AFH have the pilot confirm those tests in the aircraft records before IFR [[23:131|IFH 5-36]] [[24:40|AFH 2-3]]. Application: teach the learner to find the entry, not assume the test was done.

This Task closes the loop opened in FII.III.C (the check before flight) and IR.VIII.A (the pilot's postflight): what the preflight finds, what the flight reveals, and what the postflight records for the next preflight. Teach them as one routine.
gaps: No source here gives a standard squawk sheet or discrepancy record format; use the school's or owner's system, which the instructor should know [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

No source here says what ATC does when an IFR flight plan to a nontowered airport is never canceled. The AIM's 1/2-hour search and rescue rule is written for VFR and DVFR plans [[33:339|AIM 5-1-14]], and AIM 6-2-6 says only that ARTCCs and FSSs alert search and rescue when an aircraft is overdue [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]].
The airplane's suction range, alternator warning, standby battery and EFIS failure messages come from the POH/AFM, which is not among these sources.
AC 91-67A (MEL and deferral practice) is not a build source; the deferral rules here come from 14 CFR 91.213 and PHAK 9-9 to 9-10.
No source here defines "24 calendar months"; the PHAK defines only 12 calendar months, from any day of a month to the last day of that month the next year [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]].

activities.title: Read a vacuum failure
activities.intro: Drag each label to the instrument it describes in IFH Figure 11-8. The airplane is really level at 2,000 feet.

pins.label: Attitude indicator: shows a left bank, OFF flag
Turn coordinator: wings level, no turn

activities.why: In Figure 11-8 the airplane is level at 2,000 feet; it looks like a left turn only to a pilot who misses the OFF flags. Comparing the attitude indicator with the turn indicator and VSI finds the failure [[23:332|IFH 11-7]], and with no vacuum warning light the pilot must watch the vacuum gauge [[23:333|IFH 11-8]].

activities.title: What you saw, what you do
activities.intro: Tap an observation, then the action the sources call for.

pairs.l: CDI swings ±5° at one rpm, steady at another
pairs.r: Try a small rpm change before reporting anything

pairs.l: Garbled identifier and flag flicker on one VOR station
pairs.r: Make a user report on the NAVAID

pairs.l: ILS receiver fails under IFR in controlled airspace
pairs.r: Report to ATC as soon as practical

pairs.l: GPS anomaly on the installed IFR receiver
pairs.r: Also file the GPS Anomaly Reporting Form after the flight

pairs.l: Altimeter 90 ft off field elevation in the run-up area
pairs.r: Refer it to an instrument repair station

pairs.l: Compass error the correction card does not explain
pairs.r: Write it up so maintenance can swing it and update the card

activities.title: Can it go IFR tomorrow?
activities.intro: No MEL, small piston airplane. Sort each item from today's write-ups and records.
buckets: No IFR until fixed or tested
May be deferred if 91.213(d) is met

items.t: Attitude indicator tumbles and will not erect
Slip-skid ball stuck at one side
Static system and altimeter last tested 30 calendar months ago (IFR in controlled airspace)
VOR checked at the VOT 12 days ago, 2° error, logged and signed
Altimeter, static and encoder tested 14 months ago

activities.why: Required for IFR and not deferrable: [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)]] [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iii)]]. The 24-month test: [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(a)]]. Items not on the 91.205 list may be deferred only if type certification, the equipment list, KOEL and ADs allow, with placard and hazard determination [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]]. VOR within 30 days and ±4°: [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(a)]] [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(1)]].

activities.title: Check the numbers before you log them
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: VOT check: CDI centered with the OBS at 356° and a FROM flag. What is the bearing error in degrees?
items.why: A perfect VOT check is 0° FROM [[33:70|AIM 1-1-4]]: 360 - 356 = 4°, right at the ±4° limit, so it passes [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(1)]].

items.q: With no VOT or ground checkpoint at the departure airport, your learner uses an airborne checkpoint published as the 090° radial; the receiver shows 097°. What is the error in degrees?
items.why: 7° is over the ±6° airborne limit [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(3)]], so IFR flight must not be attempted until the error is corrected [[33:71|AIM 1-1-4]].

items.q: Dual VORs tuned to the same station show bearings of 213° and 217°. What is the difference in degrees?
items.why: 4° is the maximum permissible variation between the two [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(c)]], so it passes, and it is logged [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]].

items.q: Field elevation 1,180 ft. With the current setting, the altimeter reads 1,265 ft in the run-up area. What is the error in feet?
items.why: 1,265 - 1,180 = 85 ft, more than 75 ft even after the run-up recheck, so refer it to a repair station [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].

items.q: Using the correction card in Figure 8-35 (this lesson's compass card figure), what compass heading do you steer for 090° with the radios on?
items.why: The card shows FOR 090, STEER 095 with radios on (094 with radios off) [[1:227|PHAK 8-25]].

activities.title: True or false: closing the loop
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: After a mechanic replaces the attitude indicator, the airplane may fly before the return-to-service entry is made.
cards.why: False. It needs approval for return to service and the 43.9 or 43.11 entry first [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(a)]].

cards.s: After a static line is opened and closed, the static system must be tested again before IFR in controlled airspace.
Using the alternate static valve in flight means the static system must be retested.
cards.why: False. The rule excepts use of the drains and the alternate static valve [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(a)(2)]].

cards.s: A 91.213(d) deferral is the way to handle an instrument that fails in flight.
cards.why: False. Deferrals are not used for in-flight discrepancies; use the AFM/POH procedures [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]].

cards.s: With an MEL, the records available to the pilot must describe the inoperable items.
The owner may throw away the inspector's discrepancy list at the next annual, even if the items are not fixed.
cards.why: False. It is kept until the defects are repaired and the airplane is approved for return to service [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(b)(3)]].

cards.s: If you know your receiver reads 2° high, you may subtract 2° from the VOR check result.
cards.why: False. No correction other than the manufacturer's correction card figures may be applied [[33:71|AIM 1-1-4]].

cards.s: When a repair station test signal is used, the repair station also enters the bearing it transmitted and the date.

activities.title: Run the debrief in order
activities.intro: Put the AIH debrief steps in order, first to last, then tap Check.
steps: Replay: the learner tells the flight back while you listen
Reconstruct: what she would, could or should have done differently
Reflect: what she learned, what was hardest, what was uncomfortable
Redirect: link today's lesson to other experiences and the next session
Compare her self-assessment with your own notes and discuss
activities.why: The four-step self-assessment is from [[25:136|AIH 6-5]]; collaborative assessment then compares the instructor's assessment with the learner's [[25:182|AIH 9-12]] [[25:138|AIH 6-7]].

activities.title: An IFR training flight, start to finish
activities.intro: You are the CFII on an IFR training flight. Make each call as the day unfolds.

steps.s: En route in IMC, the suction needle drops below the green and the attitude indicator starts to drift in turns. What do you have your learner do first?
options: Keep flying the attitude indicator and write it up after landing
Cross-check it with the turn coordinator and VSI; advise ATC
Pull the vacuum pump's circuit breaker and continue as planned
Cover the turn coordinator so she practices on the full panel
steps.why: Compare the attitude indicator with the turn indicator and VSI to identify the failure, keep control on the working instruments, then advise ATC and declare an emergency if needed [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].

steps.s: ATC clears you for the approach to a nontowered field. Below 2,000 feet it is VFR, and you know your radio cannot reach ATC on the ground there.
options: Cancel IFR by radio on the ground after landing
Leave it open; it closes itself at the field
Cancel airborne while in contact, if the rest can be VFR
Ask other traffic on the CTAF to relay the cancellation to Center
steps.why: With no FSS or radio contact on the ground, cancel while still airborne and able to talk to ATC, weather permitting [[33:340|AIM 5-1-15]], and be certain the rest of the flight can be VFR [[23:294|IFH 10-3]].

steps.s: After landing, the attitude indicator looks normal and your learner says there is nothing to write up.
options: Agree, since it passed the taxi check and works now
Write it up: conditions, times, suction and what it did
Tell the next renter in person, but leave the sheet blank
Placard it INOP yourself and log it as deferred for IFR
steps.why: Describe it the way the AIM's anomaly report does [[33:87|AIM 1-1-13]] [[33:88|AIM 1-1-13]], in the discrepancy record [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]. An attitude indicator is required for IFR [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(8)]], so it cannot be deferred for IFR [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iii)]].

steps.s: Next morning a club member wants the airplane for an IFR trip. Your squawk is still open, with no maintenance entry.
options: Maintenance checks it first; no IFR until signed off
He may go IFR if the gyro erects normally on his run-up
He may go IFR with a placard and a handheld backup
He may go IFR if you sign a 91.213(d) deferral
steps.why: The pilot in command decides airworthiness [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7(b)]], an attitude indicator is required for IFR and cannot be deferred [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(8)]] [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iii)]], and after maintenance the return-to-service entry must exist [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(a)]]. "Probably okay" is the cue to revisit the consequences [[1:56|PHAK 2-17]].

steps.s: In the debrief, your learner rates her partial-panel work as "Perform." You saw her lose 200 feet.
options: Change her rating to "Practice" yourself and move on
Have her replay and reconstruct it, then compare ratings
Skip the rating, since this debrief is only for squawks
Accept her rating to protect her confidence
steps.why: Replay and Reconstruct let her find the gap herself [[25:136|AIH 6-5]]; then compare her rating with yours and discuss, as in the AIH rubric example [[25:138|AIH 6-7]].
